title: An Act relating to data centers; and relating to utility service for data centers

latestAction.text: (H) Read the first time; referred to House Community & Regional Affairs

summary: Bars electric and gas utilities from putting into general rates any cost they would not have incurred but for serving a data center, unless those rates recover the cost solely from the data center. Requires a Regulatory Commission of Alaska-approved service contract for each data center. The contract must account for data-center infrastructure, assign its cost directly to the data center, and not increase fuel-supply risk for any utility. Transmission built specifically for a data center is kept out of the backbone transmission cost pool at first.
significance: A strict cost-causation model for Railbelt utilities facing hyperscale inquiries amid Cook Inlet gas-supply concerns. It passed the Senate 14-5 on reconsideration (2026-05-16) but was only referred in the House before the 34th Legislature's final session adjourned.

title: Electric Utilities; review by Public Service Commission of certain contracts with large load data centers further provided for

latestAction.text: Approved by Governor (Act 2026-610)

committees: Senate Fiscal Responsibility and Economic Development
summary: Adds Code of Alabama 37-4-22.1. Contracts between a utility and a large load data center are in the public interest only if the cost of supplying the data center is recouped from it and the contract promotes positive benefits for other retail customers. In judging benefits, the PSC considers whether the terms could lower other customers' costs, whether the data center increases system efficiency, and whether it contributes to local economic growth. Reporting says it applies to loads of 150 MW or more in Alabama Power's territory.
significance: Alabama's first statutory data-center cost-causation standard, aimed at Alabama Power's hyperscale contracts. It passed nearly unanimously (House 100-1, Senate concurrence 33-0, per reporting).

title: To amend the sales and use tax exemption for data centers

latestAction.text: Notification that HB1444 is now Act 548

summary: Expands Arkansas's data center sales and use tax exemption (Ark. Code 26-52-456). Cuts the qualified data center investment threshold from $500 million to $100 million within five years of construction start. Creates a 'qualified large data center' tier for multi-site, fiber-linked campuses with $2 billion in investment within 10 years and $3 million in annual compensation. Broadens exempt equipment to include power storage, cooling, water conservation systems, modular data centers and labor services, and keeps the exemption on electricity used. Excludes crypto-mining facilities. Moves administration to the Department of Finance and Administration, with certificate revocation if investment or payroll commitments are missed.
significance: A significant loosening of Arkansas's incentive that makes far smaller projects eligible and adds a hyperscale multi-site tier. It positions the state to compete for large campuses.

Among other provisions, electrical corporations with more than 250,000 customers must file PSC tariff schedules for customers projected to exceed 100 MW of annual peak demand (50 MW for smaller utilities). Those schedules must make such customers pay a representative share of the costs of serving them and keep other classes from bearing unjust or unreasonable costs. The act also makes a range of other utility ratemaking and planning changes.
significance: Made Missouri one of the first states to require large-load (data-center) tariffs by statute. The largest investor-owned utilities must now file large-load tariffs with the PSC.

title: Creating the Right to Compute Act and requiring shutdowns of AI controlled critical infrastructure

latestAction.text: Chapter Number Assigned (Chapter 150); signed by Governor 2025-04-16

summary: Establishes a statutory right to own and use computational resources; any government action restricting that right must be demonstrably necessary and narrowly tailored to a compelling government interest. significance: First enacted 'right to compute' law in the U.S. and a template (ALEC-style) for other states; raises the legal bar for state or local restrictions on computing infrastructure, which data-center developers may invoke against restrictive measures.

title: Adopt the Large Load Customer Regulation Act, provide for eminent domain relating to energy storage and regulation and taxation of energy storage resources, and change provisions relating to cryptocurrency mining operations and data centers

latestAction.text: Approved by Governor on April 14, 2026

summary: Adopts the Large Load Customer Regulation Act for new or expanded loads over 20 MW at one site. Public power suppliers must set interconnection standards: disclosure of competing service requests and onsite backup generation, a study fee of $50,000 or $1,000/MW (whichever is greater), proof of site control, and financial commitments for new transmission and generation. Suppliers may set rates that fairly allocate system costs to large loads and must have procedures to procure load flexibility and require curtailment or backup-generator deployment in grid emergencies. For data centers of 10 MW or more, suppliers may require direct payment or a letter of credit for upgrades and full-cost service terms. Operators must file annual reports with the Department of Water, Energy, and Environment and the Natural Resources Committee (electricity demand, water use, tax exemptions, incentives, efficiency, renewable commitments), bear decommissioning costs, and enter community benefit agreements. Also folds in LB1111, LB1064 and LB1193 and taxes energy storage by nameplate capacity.
significance: Nebraska's comprehensive data-center law for its all-public-power system. It pairs cost-causation tools for OPPD, NPPD and LES with mandatory water and energy disclosure and community benefit agreements. It passed 49-0.

summary: Creates alternative ways to serve large electrical loads. Large-load customers (e.g., data centers) can contract for service through qualified utilities or third-party large-scale generation providers, partly exempt from standard rate regulation. Sets up closed private generation and connected generation systems, adds accounting and transparency requirements to protect retail customers, and directs the PSC to study a flexible large-load tariff and review the program periodically.
significance: Utah's main framework for hyperscale and AI campuses. It lets them bring or contract their own generation outside Rocky Mountain Power's standard rate base and adds ratepayer-protection accounting.
